chapter_theme: Civakan routs the hunters who seized the cowherds' herd, turning it back by the sound of his bow with no man lost; the city hails him as an Arjuna, and its women throng the street in a long scene of longing, praising his mother's penance, praying for him in dreams and paling as his chariot passes, until he enters his home and the chariot is housed with offerings.

cast.role: the hero, raised by the merchant Kantukkatan, who recovers the seized herd
the hunters who seized the cowherds' herd, also called கானவர்
the cowherds whose herd is recovered
the usurping ruler, taken here as the one angered by the news
the women of the city who throng the street to see Civakan

451.reading: As wind rising in a line blows apart the dark rain that falls clinging to a great hill, the prince with his bow, which spits arrows in a row, wards off the rain of hot-tipped arrows the hunters loose in ranks.
451.event: The hunters shower arrows on Civakan, and he parries them with his own arrows.

452.reading: As the foresters flee before the fierce arrows set to his bow, the herd turns back and the cowherds shout, while of the matchless archer's strong shoulders one bends and one straightens, so that he is said to stand like a cloud raining arrows.
452.event: The hunters flee, the herd turns back and the cowherds cheer Civakan.
452.nuance: The rhythm of the drawing arm, one shoulder bowed and one straight, is the poet's picture of continuous shooting; the herd is not driven back by him but turns of itself once the raiders run.

453.reading: When the six thousand hunters, with five hundred at their head, rain arrows by hundreds on his body, he cuts away the bows and arrows in their hands, and in a moment they vanish as the minds of kohl-eyed women do.
453.event: Civakan cuts down the hunters' bows and arrows and the hunters vanish.
453.nuance: The count in line 1 can be read as six thousand under five hundred leaders or as six thousand five hundred. மாய்ந்தார் may mean they perished or that they vanished from the field; the simile of women's changing minds, the epic's own view of women here, favours vanishing, and the next verse speaks of no blade drawing blood.

454.reading: With neither the edge of a sword nor the point of an arrow, the young man turns back the herd by the mere twang of the bow on his shoulder and returns, like the full white moon that the tall god freed from the planet's mouth.
454.event: Civakan recovers the herd by the sound of his bow and comes back.
454.nuance: Line 1 does not say whose body went unwounded: it can mean the recovery cost the hunters no blood or that Civakan came back untouched; the moon released whole from Rahu fits either. The god is named only as நெடியான், the tall one.

455.reading: When word comes that, with no man of his lost, he of the blooming garland with his companions has recovered the seized herd of the cowherd, one who heard it raged like a man whose last day had come, as if a spear had been thrown into a sword wound, and the city roared.
455.event: News of the recovery reaches the city, which cheers, while one who hears it rages.
455.nuance: The one who rages (வெகுண்டான்) is not named; that he is Kattiyankaran, whose rule Civakan's success shames, is a reading from the story so far, not from the verse. கோவன் here is the herd's owner, not Civakan.

456.reading: The townspeople spread incense smoke over the sun-touching bannered mansions, scatter powder, hang flower garlands, sprinkle scent and, holding garlands, hail the young man as like the young hero of the horse chariot who wasted the wide army of the snake-bannered king, saying 'may he flourish'.
456.event: The city decorates its streets and blesses Civakan on his return.
456.nuance: The comparison is to the Mahabharata: the snake banner is Duryodhana's, and the hero who routed his host is Arjuna, who in that story too recovered seized cattle; the poet sets the merchant's foster son beside an epic prince.

457.reading: Women with red mouths like sweet nectar, the lisping speech of young parrots and rising breasts spotted with gold-bright freckles run to see the young man until their lightning waists ache, and fill the street like swans and peacocks.
457.event: The young women of the city run into the street to see Civakan.

458.reading: With the small drums of their anklets sounding, their hips decked as golden chariots yoked to the horses of their breasts, their long eyes as arrows and their brows as bows bent, Kama's army rises against the young lord.
458.nuance: The whole verse is a war in reverse: the hero just home from routing an army now meets one made of the women's bodies, and it is he who is the target.

459.reading: Binding in their bodices the fiery breasts that swell till their waists, finer than thread, bend, and holding garlands in fingers reddened by the plectrum, they stand waiting for him to come, like the women of the gods.

460.reading: Women with wide flower-like eyes, standing half hidden with only their breasts that bring forth pleasure and wealth showing, look like the daughters of the Nagas risen from their underworld.

461.reading: All the wide flower eyes, long beyond men's measure, like two whetted spears met in fight, crowd together along the street where his chariot goes, as nerunji flowers with their rows of petals turn to watch the course of the sun.

462.reading: Shawls, silks, ear-rolls, garlands, gems, pearls, bracelets, earrings and jewels mingle their light, and as if lightning were ranged along the old city's every boundary, every mansion brings forth women with hips like a snake's hood.

463.reading: Peacock-like women speak the customary words of blessing, some calling him a young elephant of a man and some wishing that he wed the earth too, and they shower powder everywhere, toss cool pollen-dropping garlands and stand flinging sandal paste.
463.event: The women bless Civakan with auspicious words and shower him with powder, garlands and sandal.
463.nuance: பூமியும் புணர்க, 'may he join the earth too', is a wedding blessing that makes rule a second bride; the women do not know he is the dead king's son. போதகம் in line 2 is taken as the elephant calf; the sense of the epithet is not certain.

464.reading: Others stand worshipping, saying that all the learned who walk in the fruitful subtle books have told of one unequalled in giving and one in sword-fighting crueller than killing Death, and all that we have seen in Nambi Civakan of the garland.
464.event: Women worship Civakan as the one in whom the books' ideal of giver and warrior is seen.

claims.claim: the learned books name the unequalled giver and the unequalled warrior as the highest of men

464.nuance: The pairing of கொடை and படை repeats the Sangam measure of a man, the patron and the fighter, and the women make Civakan the proof of the books rather than the books the measure of him.

465.reading: Some say the good mother who bore this lord must have done penance; some ask on which mountain she did it, so that they too may attain the like; and women with nectar breasts, dried up within, stare at him and tell their friends of the burning sickness they suffer.
465.event: Women praise Civakan's mother's penance and tell their friends of their longing.

claims.claim: bearing such a son is the fruit of a mother's past penance

465.nuance: எய்துவம் யாமும் leaves open what they hope to attain, a son like him or the man himself; the next lines on their longing lean to the second.

466.reading: Some ask that the lord who overcame the angry hunters grace them by coming in a dream tomorrow and showing his red flower-like chest so they may see it, while others, bewildered in their minds, stand saying what they want with no one asking them.
466.event: Women pray that Civakan visit them in a dream, and others voice their desires unasked.

467.reading: They say none on earth matches this lord of the victorious spear, perhaps only those in heaven, and wonder who they might be, the poor fortunate ones, whose penance has given them the elephant-like hero so that women whose words dwell in music may drink his beauty.

claims.claim: union with such a man is gained as the reward of penance

467.nuance: அளியர் can be pity or envy ('poor things' or 'blessed ones'), and whether the penance is the women's or their families' is not stated. யார்கொலோ அளியர் is the Sangam turn of wonder at a hero (Purananuru 257 has யார்கொலோ அளியன்), here moved from the hero to the women who would have him.

468.reading: The moment they see the generous one in his bordered garment, the coins of their silk girdles slip round their soft feet, their lac-red mouths scorch, and they stand burning in the fierce fire of desire with the bangles sliding off their hands.

469.reading: As the women with swelling breasts watch him go, praising his bearing and worshipping him, their shoulders droop, and on this side bangles shower to the ground, so that the street where the lord's chariot runs turns pale as the beerkan flower.
469.nuance: The pallor of longing, which akam poetry lays on one woman's skin, is spread here over a whole street; the chariot leaves a pale track behind it.

470.reading: Tilting their rain-flower eyes as if to drink the young man and cure the pallor on their shoulders, the women stand trembling, held back by the noose of shame; he, like a fierce-faced tiger, does not stop, and enters his rich walled home.
470.event: Civakan passes the women without stopping and enters his walled home.
470.nuance: Shame (நாண்) holds the women where they stand, and the hero's not stopping (நிற்ப நில்லான்) is set against their standing; the sequence of the crowd scene ends in one line of his action.

471.reading: The horses unyoked from the golden yoke go into their stalls, people fill gem bowls wishing that his victory last, and bearing sweet offerings of liquor, flowers, sandal and lamps, the shining chariot is brought into its gold-bright shed.
471.event: The horses are stabled and the chariot is housed with offerings for lasting victory.
471.nuance: மதுப் பலி, an offering of liquor or honey, is made to the victorious chariot; the verse gives no sign of any Jain reserve about it.

links.note: The patikam's line வஞ்சம் மறவர் நிரை வள்ளல் விடுத்த வாறும் announces that the liberal one freed the herd from deceitful hunters; 451 to 455 tell it, ending with the herd turned by the bow's sound and no man lost.
links.teaches: The patikam's word வள்ளல் for the rescuer of a herd only makes sense once the telling shows a recovery that is given back to its owners without loss, so the summary's epithet anticipates the bloodless manner of the deed.

links.note: The city women bless the unknown youth with பூமியும் புணர்க, 'may he wed the earth too'; the patikam's verse 26 puts his marriage to his uncle's daughter and the spread of his umbrella and sceptre over the land in one verse.
links.teaches: The epic pairs bride and kingdom twice, once as a crowd's wedding blessing on a merchant's son who does not know his birth and once as the outcome, so the blessing works as an unwitting prophecy of his recovery of the throne.

links.note: The women hold that union with Civakan is the reward of penance (அண்ணலைத் தவத்திற் றந்தார்); the patikam ends with Civakan, as one who has eaten nectar, no longer wanting the pleasure of women.
links.teaches: The epic plants early the crowd's belief that penance buys the pleasure of this man, and its own close makes the same man's penance the end of all such pleasure, so the word தவம் is turned against the hope it first expressed.

links.note: In the Vettuva Vari the herds the hunters' brothers brought back from the raid fill the yards of the smith, the drummer and the yazh bards; in the Cintamani the hunters are routed and the herd turns back to the shouting cowherds.
links.teaches: Held together, the two epics show the one cattle raid from both ends: the Silappathikaram's hunters' seizure feeds a whole village of dependents, while the Cintamani's recovery returns the same kind of herd to its keepers and leaves the raiders faceless.

links.note: The Purananuru's warrior, with no chariot and no forest fort, watched the enemy's herd go, counted it and turned it with his bow (சிலையின் மாற்றியோனே); Civakan turns the herd by the bow's twang alone (சிலையின் னொலியால் தொறு மீட்டு).
links.teaches: The epic keeps the Sangam feat of turning a herd with the bow but removes even the drawn arrow and gives the deed to a city's darling, so a poor warrior's unsung skill becomes a prince's proof of worth before the town.

gains.a: the Cintamani's bow-sound recovery is shown to rest on an existing heroic type, the lone bowman who turns a herd, rather than on the poet's invention
gains.b: the Puram poem's quiet single-handed recovery is seen to be the seed of a scene that later poetry could magnify into public triumph and crowd adoration

links.note: Kural 265 says penance (செய்தவம்) is undertaken because what one wants is got as one wants it; the city women say Civakan's mother must have done penance (செய்தவம் உடையள்) and ask on which mountain to do it so that they too may attain.
links.teaches: The couplet's frank promise that penance gets what one wants is taken literally by lovesick townswomen, who plan austerity on a mountain to win a man, showing how the Kural's motive can be bent toward the very desire the next couplet condemns.

gains.a: the women's talk is shown to repeat a recognised ethical doctrine of the fruits of penance, not merely a crowd's fancy
gains.b: the couplet's unqualified wording is shown to license a use, penance for erotic gain, that its own chapter would reject

links.note: In Kural 1214 the woman finds pleasure in dreams because they bring the man who gives no grace when she is awake (நல்காரை); the women of 466 ask Civakan to grace them (அருளி) by coming in a dream tomorrow.
links.teaches: The Kural's dream comforts a woman for a lover who once was hers and now withholds himself, but the Cintamani's crowd asks the dream for a man they have only seen pass, so the convention turns from consolation for loss into the only union a stranger can hope for.

gains.a: the crowd's prayer is shown to draw on the akam convention that the dream does what the absent man will not
gains.b: the couplet's dream-remedy is shown stretching beyond separation to love that never had a meeting, which the couplet's situation does not cover

source_issues: 456, 461, 469 (lines 2 and 4) and 471: the tool repaired a TSCII slip (ோ் read as ேர்); the repaired readings (தேர், ஏர்) fit the sense.
451 and 452 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the tool.
453 line 1: ஐந்நூறு நூறு தலையிட்ட ஆறாயிரவர் can be counted two ways (six thousand under five hundred, or six thousand five hundred).
